Central to his work is the belief that existence is never a solitary state but is continuously formed through the "encounter of two or more." Whether exploring the relationship between canvas and pigment or the observer and the observed, Yang visualizes the world as a dynamic structure of interconnectedness.

Since night views are defined by the interplay of light and shadow outlining objects, the depiction of light is the core focus of his work. park-hyung-jin-2.bio: Park Hyung-jin was born in Seoul, Korea in 1968. Park has been working on the concept of "Everything is connected" since 1994, exploring the content of Korean shamanism. The artist often works by going into the mountains, feeling the colors of natural life, breathing in the clean air, and experiencing the cycle of nature. The human-created framework of society is also considered to be part of the cycle of nature, which is also part of the cycle of the universe, and has been continuing his work.

sungmi-lee-1.name: Sungmi Lee
sungmi-lee-1.bio: Sungmi Lee creates dreamlike images by working with the physicality of materials and a range of media. Embracing the organic, ever-shifting nature of their materials, they allow chance to generate unique shapes and rich colour combinations. This process uncovers quiet moments from everyday life and the emotions beneath them, offering a space to pause, breathe and hold on to a sense of rest and hope.

kim-byungkwan-1.name: Kim Byungkwan
kim-byungkwan-1.bio:
Byungkwan Kim was born in Seoul, South Korea and graduated in Fine Arts from the University of Hansung. 
Described as a modern Expressionist and widely recognised as one of the finest painters in contemporary art today, Byungkwan paints from images of well-known figures – Hollywood starlets, political dictators – transforming their familiar faces into strange and disconcerting paintings. His expressive paintings stop us in our tracks and challenge us to step outside what he terms “visual habit.”

kyunghwa-park.name: Kyunghwa Park
kyunghwa-park.bio:
In the fleeting currents of ordinary days, I gather small glimmers of light. My work holds onto the fading glow of childhood innocence and captures the breath of nature as it dims with time.

Using luminous colors, I depict the persistence of life that shines even in the darkness, breathing precious narratives into the smallest existences, such as a vanishing bee. Blooming a quiet fantasy at the boundary of reality and imagination, I hope my canvas offers a gentle solace to the viewer’s heart.

Through sleepers, charcoal, asphalt concrete, and mixed stones - materials in which have been thrown away in contemporary society – the true side of human being is revealed. Chung Hyun does not alter the material much, but he tends to correspond and try not to lose any of the material’s particular characteristics, rather concentrates on bringing out power carried within out onto the surface.

chun-kyungja.bio:
Chun Kyung-ja (1924–2015) is one of the most celebrated and commercially significant figures in modern Korean art history. Known as the "Magician of Color," Chun broke away from the male-dominated traditions of East Asian ink wash painting to pioneer a vivid, surrealistic style of "Chae-saek-hwa" (Korean color painting). Her work is instantly recognizable for its bold use of primary colors, layered mineral pigments, and hauntingly expressive portraits.

seo-in-jung.bio:
My practice explores the profound intersection of destruction and creation through the transformative power of fire on Hanji (traditional Korean mulberry paper). By utilizing fire as a surrogate for the traditional brush and ink, I engage in a ritualistic process where burning and extinguishing paradoxically yield new forms. This method subverts the conventional act of filling a canvas; instead, I "burn" to counteract the void, accumulating charred layers to give tangible shape to emptiness.

yunju-park.name: Yunju Park
yunju-park.bio:
To exist by one’s own rhythm, unshaken by the currents of the world.
I focus on an aesthetic that knows how to linger in emptiness—an attitude of accepting the flow without haste and living in harmony with nature.
Such a perspective has long permeated daily life, shaping a uniquely Korean sensibility.
The subjects in my work are reflections of our own lives and the emotions we encounter; they serve as mediums that embody our attitude toward life.

Her choice to depict the seascape using soil may seem unconventional, yet it evokes a longstanding symbolic connection between earth and water as primal substances associated with maternity and origin. In particular, the sea—unfixed, ever-shifting, and ceaseless in its cycles of emergence and dissolution—evokes the transience of life and the limits of human existence.

hyegyun-kim.name: Hyegyun Kim
hyegyun-kim.bio:
Kim Hye-Gyun articulates the multifaceted scenes of everyday life—familiar yet often overlooked—through sculptural objects arranged on shelves. Her works consistently feature rounded, endearing human figures alongside various everyday objects. These figures evoke the form of a roly-poly toy or resemble Matryoshka dolls, in which one figure is nested within another.
In her practice, the doll functions as a central motif symbolizing both the origin of existence and the relational nature of being.

lee-bae.name: Lee Bae
lee-bae.bio: For much of his career, Korean modernist Lee Bae worked almost exclusively with charcoal. Focusing on this single material, he created monochromatic linear drawings, canvases that featured embedded charcoal shards, and large-scale sculptures derived from carbonized tree trunks. Recently, Lee has embraced resin, ink, and acrylics as expanded avenues of materiality. Texture and gesture remain major aesthetic concerns. Lee received his MFA from the Hongik University Graduate School of Art in Seoul.

seungtaik-jang.name: Seungtaik Jang
seungtaik-jang.bio: Seung-Taik Jang is a Korean Asian Modern & Contemporary artist who was born in 1959 in Goyang, Korea. He studied in Hongik University, Seoul, Korea and Ecole Nationale Superieure des Arts Decoratifs de Paris, France. His work was featured in several exhibitions at key galleries and museums in Korea. Public collections of his works involve National Museum of Contemporary Art, Seoul Metropolitan Art Museum, Seoul National University and more.

jian-yoo.name: Jian Yoo
jian-yoo.bio:
Jian Yoo (South Korean, b. 1982) explores how invisible flows of time and emotion take form as structures through light, material, and space. Emotion is understood as the most delicate trace of existence and the most private record of time. 

Accumulated time, shifting emotions, and traces of experience continuously circulate—gathering, dispersing, and moving. These flows are not depicted but take form as structures that can be perceived through the senses.

choi-yeong-geol.name: Choi Yeong Geol
choi-yeong-geol.bio:
Choi Yeong-Geol is trained in Oriental painting and is recognized for his realistic depictions of nature, achieved through meticulous observation and a profound sense of empathy. While his works are grounded in traditional techniques, they clearly diverge from conventional modes of classical landscape painting. In this way, his practice embodies a balance between tradition and modernity, as well as between academic rigor and a romantic sensibility.
